summary: Children aged 9–10 learn to see fraction addition and subtraction as JOINING and SEPARATING the same unit parts, with the denominator (the unit) held fixed throughout. The central skill is decomposing a fraction into a sum of same-denominator parts in MORE THAN ONE way (5/6 = 1/6+4/6 = 2/6+3/6 = 1/6+1/6+3/6), and expressing a mixed number as a single count of like parts (2 1/8 = 8/8+8/8+1/8 = 17/8). The aim is to shift from 'apply the numerator rule' to 'a fraction is a flexible collection of unit parts I can split and recombine', which later makes mixed-number arithmetic, common denominators, and regrouping in subtraction coherent rather than separate tricks.
misconceptions: Alters denominators when decomposing (a reverse add-across): writes 5/6 = 2/3 + 3/3 because 2+3=5 and 3+3=6, so the parts don't actually total 5/6.
Believes a fraction has only one 'correct' break-up (3/8 must be 1/8+1/8+1/8) and cannot produce a different valid decomposition.
Treats a mixed number's whole and fraction parts as disconnected numbers, unable to express 2 1/8 as a single count of eighths (17/8).

activities.title: Slice one bar many ways
steps: Start with a bar whose total length represents 5/6 of a whole, marked off into five equal sixths (each one-sixth of the whole) against a fixed ruler so its length cannot change.
Group the sixths one way (e.g. 1 and 4) and write the matching sum of sixths underneath: 5/6 = 1/6 + 4/6.
Regroup the SAME bar differently (2 and 3; then 1, 1 and 3) and write each new sum: 2/6 + 3/6, 1/6 + 1/6 + 3/6.
Line up all the sums you have written against the single unchanged bar and say aloud: 'all of these are 5/6'.
Repeat the whole process with a fresh fraction you have not seen (e.g. 7/8) to produce at least two distinct decompositions.
activities.insight: A fraction is not one fixed break-up: any grouping of its unit parts that uses the same denominator and the same total count measures the same quantity. Addition joins those parts and subtraction separates them, while the unit stays fixed.

activities.title: Mixed number as one count of like parts
steps: Lay out 2 1/8 as two whole bars, each cut into eight eighths, plus one extra eighth.
Count the eighths in each whole bar (8/8 and 8/8), then join the extra eighth.
Write the quantity as a single count of eighths: 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8, confirming the 2 wholes contribute 16/8, not 2/8.
State in words why the whole and the fraction are one quantity: 2 1/8 is seventeen eighths altogether.
activities.insight: A mixed number's whole part and fraction part are the same kind of unit part; the wholes can be recounted as eighths so the whole quantity is a single count of like parts (17/8).

activities.title: Check and sort candidate decompositions
steps: Given several candidate sums for 5/6, decide which equal 5/6 and which do not — e.g. 1/6+4/6, 2/6+3/6, and the trap 2/3+3/3.
For each candidate, add the parts and compare the total to 5/6 to justify the decision, not just guess.
Explain why 2/3 + 3/3 fails: adding them gives 5/3 (more than a whole), not 5/6, and the parts are not measured in sixths.
Fill in a second valid decomposition of a given fraction, and match each mixed number to its improper form (e.g. 2 1/8 ↔ 17/8).
activities.insight: A valid same-denominator decomposition must keep the denominator fixed AND have parts that actually total the original fraction; the reverse add-across (2/3+3/3 because 2+3=5 and 3+3=6) produces parts that do not sum to 5/6.

activities.title: Explain, don't just compute, subtraction as separating
steps: Show 5/6 − 2/6 on a bar or number line by separating two sixths from five sixths and reading the remaining three sixths.
Say in words what subtraction did: it separated two of the same unit parts, leaving 3/6; the denominator (sixths) did not change.
Connect it to joining: 3/6 + 2/6 rebuilds the original 5/6, so joining and separating are opposite moves on the same unit parts.
activities.insight: Subtraction separates like unit parts just as addition joins them; the denominator names the unit and stays fixed, so only the count of parts changes.

checkQuestion: Show me TWO different ways to break 5/6 into a sum of sixths. Then take 2 1/8 and write it as a sum that includes its whole parts — show it however helps you (a picture, a number line, or numbers).
checkAnswer: 5/6 = e.g. 1/6 + 4/6 AND 2/6 + 3/6 (any two distinct sums of sixths totalling 5/6). 2 1/8 = 1 + 1 + 1/8 = 8/8 + 8/8 + 1/8 = 17/8. Denominator stays sixths/eighths throughout.
